subject: Bilal Ahmad
description: Verified public-profile knowledge used by Ask Mintorian. Records are authored from the Mintorian website and the public CV included in this repository.

records.title: Professional and research profile
records.summary: Bilal Ahmad is a PhD student at the University of Bath whose work combines power-system reliability, battery energy storage systems and machine-learning-enabled decision support. Alongside his research, he holds two part-time Full Stack Developer roles and previously served as a Technical Lead in machine learning at HCL Technologies.
details: His research combines data-driven learning with physically interpretable models.
The stated goals include grid resilience, flexibility and transparent decision support.
His profile spans academic research, electrical engineering, applied machine learning and software engineering.
His two current part-time, remote Full Stack Developer roles are at Dystil.AI and Just Jutz; both are listed from April 2026 to present.

records.title: Core research focus
records.summary: Bilal researches power-system reliability, battery energy storage systems (BESS), optimal power flow and security-constrained optimal power flow (OPF/SCOPF), and explainable AI for intelligent contingency screening.
details: The work focuses on energy-system operations and planning.
It uses machine learning alongside physically interpretable power-system models.
Distribution-network resilience, uncertainty and adverse-weather preparedness are recurring themes.

records.title: Clean-energy and SDG 7 alignment
records.summary: Bilal's public profile states that his research supports UN Sustainable Development Goal 7: Affordable and Clean Energy and the transition toward smarter, more efficient energy systems.
details: This is a stated research alignment; it does not by itself establish a formal United Nations affiliation or endorsement.

records.title: The Research page
records.summary: Mintorian has a Research page at /research/ collecting the parts of Bilal's work a visitor can pick up and use rather than only read about. It hosts three interactive demonstrations: whether resilience and grid limits change a site's net-zero investment, an N-1 contingency screen on the IEEE 14-bus system, and a battery siting study on a 33-bus distribution feeder driven by live GB data.
details: The page states that more will appear there as it becomes publishable. Do not name or promise any item that is not listed on it today.
This page replaced the earlier Research Group page. The old /researchgroup/ address now redirects here, so link to /research/ rather than to the old path.
All three demonstrations run entirely in the visitor's browser and need JavaScript, and all three use the same Newton-Raphson AC power-flow solver.

records.title: Does resilience change the investment? - interactive site demonstration
records.summary: The Research page opens with a demonstration asking whether engineering requirements change a site's net-zero investment. For a representative distribution warehouse it compares three pathways - the existing arrangement, the cheapest plan that meets a carbon target on energy and carbon figures alone, and the same plan once it must also fit the grid connection, pass an AC power flow on the site network and carry essential load through an outage - and states what, if anything, changed.
details: The warehouse is synthetic and its load recipe is published in the case file. The weather, solar output (PVGIS, 2023) and half-hourly GB grid carbon intensity (Carbon Intensity API, 2023) are real, and prices, emission factors and costs come from DESNZ and other cited sources, with every assumption labelled.

It is a sketch of a method, not the method, and not Bilal's research method or results. The planning is a sweep over candidate plans on representative days rather than an optimisation, it does not choose investment timing, and its two outage scenarios are named days rather than a model of compound weather. The page says so. Never describe it as his framework or as evidence of how his work performs.

The visitor changes four settings: the ride-through requirement, whether the outage is independent of the weather or correlated with a heatwave, an 800 kVA or 1,200 kVA grid connection, and whether a new diesel generator is allowed. The page re-plans all three pathways and computes a sentence saying what changed.

Two results come from the physics rather than from choices made in the demonstration: a battery bought to trade is expensive to hold in reserve, so resilience changes how it is run as much as what is bought; and a battery shaves kilowatts but not kilovars, so a plan built to a kilowatt limit can still breach its kVA connection, which the AC power flow catches and returns to the plan as a tighter limit.

It is not a connection study or a business case: fault level, protection and the G99 islanding study are not modelled, and costs are indicative. Electrification equipment - heat pumps, chargers, vans - is common to the two new pathways and is not costed.
Never quote a figure or a verdict from this panel. Every number on it depends on the settings the visitor chooses. Point the visitor at the panel instead.
The page names no client, partner or collaboration, and neither should you.

records.title: Interactive N-1 contingency screen on the IEEE 14-bus system
records.summary: The Research page carries a working N-1 contingency demonstration on the IEEE 14-bus test system. A visitor clicks any circuit to trip it, a full Newton-Raphson AC power flow re-solves in the browser, and a table ranks all twenty single-line outages by a classical severity index.
details: This demonstration is deliberately the classical method, not Bilal's own research. The page says so explicitly. Never describe it as his method, his result, or evidence of how his work performs.
His research replaces an index like this one with a learned ranking that also explains why it flagged a case. The page makes no claim about how that performs, and neither should you.
The ranking uses the active-power performance index: each branch's loading raised to a high power and summed, so one badly overloaded circuit outweighs many comfortable ones.

Raising demand exposes the point of the demonstration. Around 110 per cent the index begins ordering outages wrongly, because a spread of mid-loaded branches out-scores a single genuine overload. That failure is called masking, and the page presents it as the reason the problem is still worth researching.
The solver is checked against the case's own published solution to within 0.0013 pu and converges in four iterations from a flat start.

Stated assumptions: line ratings are chosen rather than taken from the case, which lists every thermal limit as zero; the voltage band is widened to 0.94 to 1.10 pu so that the intact solution fits inside it; generation does not re-dispatch after an outage; and generator VAr limits are not enforced.
It runs entirely in the visitor's browser and needs JavaScript. The older /contingency/ address redirects to /research/#contingency.

records.title: Interactive battery siting study on a 33-bus distribution feeder
records.summary: The Research page carries a live battery siting demonstration. A visitor picks a GB distribution licence area, clicks a bus on a 33-bus radial feeder to place a battery, sets its power and energy and chooses a dispatch rule. The feeder is re-solved for every half-hour of the last twenty-four against live GB data, and the page reports whether the siting is deliverable, what it is worth and to whom, and which way the carbon moves.
details: The network is the 33-bus radial feeder of Baran and Wu, used exactly as published, and the solver reproduces its published solution. The page states plainly that this is not a real UK feeder: no GB distribution circuit is published with full impedances under a licence that could be verified. What is British is the live data driving it.

Three live sources: regional carbon intensity per distribution licence area from the National Energy System Operator's carbon API, national demand from Elexon, and the half-hourly system price from Elexon. If a feed fails the page says so rather than substituting silently.

The three dispatch rules - price-following, carbon-following and network-support - are deliberately simple heuristics. They are not optimisers and not Bilal's research, and the page says so. Never describe them as his method or as evidence of how his work performs.

Two results come from the physics rather than from any choice made in the demonstration: location dominates, because a battery near the substation displaces current that never travelled far enough to lose anything; and a battery is a load half the time, so charging at full power into a weak point can itself be the binding constraint.

Stated assumptions: nodal demand is measured nowhere and is scaled from the published case by live GB demand; the primary busbar is held at 1.02 pu rather than the published 1.00 pu, a realistic GB tap position, because at 1.00 pu the feeder is outside the statutory band at every hour of every day; thermal ratings are assumed because the case has none; the battery runs at unity power factor; the 24-hour window closes on itself so that no energy is invented; fault level is not modelled.

Network value and owner revenue are reported as two separate ledgers and never added, because in GB a distribution network operator buys flexibility rather than owning batteries or trading. The owner figure counts the system price only and the page describes it as a floor.
It is a retrospective over the last twenty-four hours that slides forward as the feeds publish. It is not a forecast, and it is not a connection study.

Never quote a figure or a verdict from this panel. Everything on it changes with live GB conditions, and a siting that reads as recommended at one moment can read differently an hour later. Point the visitor at the panel instead.

records.title: GB Grid, Right Now panel
records.summary: The Mintorian home page carries a live panel called GB Grid, Right Now, showing Great Britain's carbon intensity, where the power is coming from, and what the transmission system is metering for the current half hour. It is read from public feeds each time the page loads.
details: The two sources are the Carbon Intensity API at carbonintensity.org.uk for intensity and the national generation mix, and Elexon's BMRS data service for half-hourly metered output in MW.

The two are shown separately and never added together: the carbon-intensity mix includes embedded solar and small wind, while Elexon meters the transmission system only and so excludes that embedded generation.
No figure from this panel is in this knowledge base. Never state a current carbon intensity, generation share or metered output. Point the visitor at the panel or at the published sources instead.
The panel is live third-party grid data, not a research result of Bilal's and not a claim about his work.

records.title: PhD in Power System Reliability
records.summary: Bilal is pursuing a PhD at the University of Bath on power-system reliability.
details: The public CV describes research on power-distribution-network preparedness for severe weather events involving compound hazards.
The work includes an automated optimal-procurement strategy framework for Distribution Network Operators (DNOs).
The work applies explainable AI to intelligent contingency screening for power-system reliability.
